reviews.evidence: Section index only; no mathematical object or theorem, so empty prerequisites are correct.
Affine hull is an intersection of affine supersets and affine combinations have coefficients summing to 1; vector-space and affine-set are direct inputs.
Images and inverse images preserve convex combinations through the affine-map identity; affine-mapping and convex-set are required.
B=A+b with A linear and b in Y; the linear-map definition is the only direct input.
Line containment is defined in a vector space using the two-point line; vector-space and line definition are required.
The translate characterization uses affine sets, subtraction, and linear subspaces in a vector space.
Limit laws use the norm triangle inequality and scalar multiplication; normed-space and norm convergence are required.
The core quantifies over all vector directions and compares with metric interior; vector-space, normed-space, and interior are needed.
The lemma assumes disjoint convex sets and nonempty core and reduces to point-set and hyperplane separation; all listed inputs are used.
Balanced and absorbing are scalar properties of subsets of a vector space; vector-space alone defines them.
Scaling, sums, and maxima are proved termwise from Jensen for extended-real convex functions; listed function inputs are direct.
Closed-set laws use metric complements and closed subsets; metric, closed-set, and ambient topology definitions are required.
Open-set laws use metric balls and open subsets; metric, open-subset, and ambient topology definitions are required.
Closure monotonicity, idempotence, and union properties require metric, closed-set, closure, and topology definitions.
Interior monotonicity and intersection properties require metric, open-set, interior, and topology definitions.
The basis criterion compares a Hamel basis with linear independence; both definitions are direct.
The biconjugate is (f*)* and later requires closed convexity; function, conjugate, and closed-convex definitions are used.
The functional norm is a supremum; normed space, linear map, absolute value, and supremum are direct.
Boundedness uses metric balls for a set and sequence range; balls and metric-space definitions are required.
The Hessian theorem displays a Hessian matrix and tests its quadratic form; replaced the generic matrix edge with the exact Hessian definition.
The theorem explicitly sets X as a real vector space; added that ambient setting.
The proof explicitly invokes convexity of -ln; added the convex-function input.
The proposition assumes convex factors and concludes convexity in the Cartesian product; the componentwise convex-combination proof uses convex-set and product-space.
The epsilon proof combines the Cauchy condition with a convergent subsequence in a metric space; all four listed concepts are explicit hypotheses or proof inputs.
Taking epsilon=1 bounds the tail in one metric ball, then finitely many initial terms give a global ball; metric, Cauchy sequence, and boundedness definitions are required.
The iff proof expands B=A+b and reconstructs A(x)=B(x)-B(0); affine-mapping is the sole direct concept.
The theorem proves unique decomposition equivalent to Y=M+N and M intersection N={0}; vector-space supplies the ambient algebra.
The proof uses the reverse triangle inequality to put an open ball around every point outside the closed ball; metric, closed-set, and topology definitions are direct.
The core defines an extended-real function with convex and closed epigraph; function, convex-function, and convex-set supply those ingredients.
The proof invokes closure via convergent sequences in both directions, with metric and closed-set definitions; the listed closure theorem is a proof prerequisite.
The complement-openness proof uses metric convergence, open complements, and the closed-set definition; the listed topology targets are required.
Closedness is defined as openness of the complement in a metric space; metric-space, open-subset, and topology definitions are direct.
The equivalence translates closure into every metric ball meeting E; metric-space, closure, and ambient topology are required.
The proof selects points in balls of radius 1/n and uses metric convergence; closure, ball characterization, sequence convergence, and topology are used.
The closure is an intersection of closed supersets in a metric space; metric and topology support the construction, while closed-set is only equivalent characterization.
The theorem needs normed convex sets, interiors and closures, and interior-segment geometry to approximate common closure points; all six listed inputs are substantive.
Codimension is dim(X/L), so vector-space, linear-subspace, and quotient-space definitions are exactly required.
The result assumes codim(L)=1 and concludes X=L direct-sum span{x0}; vector-space, subspace, codimension, and direct-sum notions are used.
Completeness is defined for an ambient metric and restricted subset through Cauchy sequences converging in the subset; all three listed concepts are direct.
Part one uses convergent-implies-Cauchy and uniqueness; part two uses completeness plus closedness, so each listed input is used.
The coordinate proof reduces Euclidean Cauchy sequences to coordinate convergence and invokes complete-metric and convergence definitions; all listed prerequisites are relevant.
The theorem applies real separation to the underlying real vector space and packages the separator via its real part; vector-space, convex-set, core, and real separation are required.

Read the complete source and every direct prerequisite target. The iff theorem relates continuity of a nonzero linear functional to closed affine level sets; normed-space and closed-set definitions are the direct inputs.
Read the complete source and every direct prerequisite target. The reverse triangle inequality directly proves norm convergence from norm convergence.
Read the complete source and every direct prerequisite target. Norm convergence is defined by a normed space and a sequence, with the associated metric convergence as the stated equivalence.
Read the complete source and every direct prerequisite target. Metric epsilon-N convergence is the complete definition; metric-space is the sole prerequisite.
Read the complete source and every direct prerequisite target. The proof bounds a tail near its limit and finitely many initial terms; convergence and bounded-set definitions are required.
Read the complete source and every direct prerequisite target. The triangle-inequality epsilon proof converts convergence to the Cauchy condition; convergence and Cauchy concepts are used.

Read the complete source and every direct prerequisite target. A convex body is nonempty compact convex in finite-dimensional real vector space; vector-space, compactness, and convexity are defining inputs.
Read the complete source and every direct prerequisite target. The definition requires a real vector space and nonnegative coefficients summing to one; vector-space is sufficient.

Read the complete source and every direct prerequisite target. The conjugate is a supremum using the Euclidean inner product and extended-real conventions; function, extended reals, supremum, and inner product are direct.

Read the complete source and every direct prerequisite target. The displayed primal/dual pair uses functions, linear map, conjugates, infimum/supremum, and Fenchel-Young weak duality; all listed inputs are used.
Read the complete source and every direct prerequisite target. Convexity is defined by convexity of the epigraph in X times R; vector-space, extended reals, epigraph, and convex-set are required.
Read the complete source and every direct prerequisite target. The hull is an intersection of convex supersets in a real vector space; vector-space, convex-set, and intersection stability are direct.
Read the complete source and every direct prerequisite target. Minimality follows from the intersection construction and convexity under intersections; vector-space, hull, and convex-set are used.
Read the complete source and every direct prerequisite target. The finite-combination characterization uses a real vector space, hull minimality, convex combinations, and closure under them.

Read the complete source and every direct prerequisite target. Convexity is defined by two-point combinations in a vector space; vector-space and line-segment equivalence are the direct inputs.
Read the complete source and every direct prerequisite target. The iff proof uses the two-point convex definition and finite convex combinations; both listed concepts are necessary.

Read the complete source and every direct prerequisite target. The theorem uses convexity, slope inequalities, differentiability, and monotonic derivative on an open interval; listed prerequisites cover the convex proof inputs.
Read the complete source and every direct prerequisite target. Partial infimum uses joint convexity, vector-space structure, and a convex feasible graph supplied by the set-valued mapping definition.
Read the complete source and every direct prerequisite target. The extension uses a real vector space, convex domain, and extended-real convexity; all three are required.
Read the complete source and every direct prerequisite target. The proof substitutes the affine combination identity into Jensen; affine map, vector-space, and convex-function definitions are direct.

Read the complete source and every direct prerequisite target. The proof uses Jensen for f and phi plus monotonicity on a convex range; vector-space, convex function, and convex-set inputs are needed.
Read the complete source and every direct prerequisite target. The corollary combines monotone derivative characterization with f twice differentiable and f second derivative nonnegative.

Read the complete source and every direct prerequisite target. The equivalence rewrites every direction through Omega minus x and the absorbing scaling condition; vector-space, set translation, core, and absorbing definitions are used.
Read the complete source and every direct prerequisite target. The equality theorem uses normed-space topology, convexity, interior, core, and the interior-segment lemma in the reverse inclusion.

Read the complete source and every direct prerequisite target. Convexity of the core uses the vector-direction definition together with convexity of Omega; vector-space, convex-set, and core are direct.
Read the complete source and every direct prerequisite target. Direct sum is defined by subspaces M,N, their set sum, and zero intersection; linear-subspace is the needed prerequisite.
Read the complete source and every direct prerequisite target. The distance is an infimum of norm distances; normed-space and infimum are required, while convexity/closure are property claims.
Read the complete source and every direct prerequisite target. Domain, epigraph, and properness require a vector space and extended-real arithmetic; both listed concepts are direct.

Read the complete source and every direct prerequisite target. The continuous dual is bounded linear functionals on a normed space and pairing is evaluation; normed-space, bounded-functional, and continuity definitions are used.

Read the complete source and every direct prerequisite target. The equivalence proves epigraph convexity iff Jensen and finite combinations; convex function, vector-space, and convex-combination notions are direct.
Read the complete source and every direct prerequisite target. The theorem requires a basis definition and the extension theorem, with the axiom-of-choice assumption stated explicitly.
Read the complete source and every direct prerequisite target. The corollary applies point-subspace separation to z0/norm(z0); normed space, bounded functional, and separation are substantive.
Read the complete source and every direct prerequisite target. This entry defines the extended reals and empty-set infimum/supremum conventions; it has no prerequisite.
Read the complete source and every direct prerequisite target. Zorn extension starts from a linearly independent set and concludes a Hamel basis; independence and basis definitions are required.

Read the complete source and every direct prerequisite target. The theorem compares f and its biconjugate and characterizes closed convex functions; function, conjugate, biconjugate, and closed-convex inputs are used.
Read the complete source and every direct prerequisite target. The inequality follows from the conjugate definition, while equality cases require subdifferential; all listed inputs are used.
Read the complete source and every direct prerequisite target. The extension theorem assumes a real vector space, subspace, and seminorm and invokes sublinear Hahn-Banach domination.

Read the complete source and every direct prerequisite target. The complex extension reduces to the real seminorm theorem while preserving complex linearity; vector-space, subspace, seminorm, and real extension are required.

Hahn–Banach in normed spaces assumes a normed space, subspace, and bounded functional and concludes a norm-preserving bounded extension; the listed prerequisites match those hypotheses and the stated seminorm theorem.

The real Hahn–Banach theorem assumes a real vector space, subspace, sublinear majorant, and linear functional and concludes an extension dominated by that majorant; all listed inputs occur in the statement.
Finite Hölder assumes real finite families and conjugate exponents; the listed weighted AM–GM is the cited scalar inequality used termwise in the proof.
Integral Hölder assumes measurable functions in conjugate Lp spaces; measurable-function, Lp-space, and weighted AM–GM supply the stated hypotheses and pointwise inequality.
A hyperplane is defined as an affine set of codimension one, with its direction subspace supplied by the parallel-subspace construction; the four listed algebraic inputs are defining.

The level-set characterization assumes a real vector space and proves both directions using hyperplanes, kernels of nonzero functionals, and codimension one; each listed concept is part of the theorem structure.
Core idempotence is stated for a convex subset of a vector space and uses the algebraic-interior operator; vector-space, convex-set, and core are the direct inputs.
The entry defines image, kernel, and linear isomorphism for a linear operator; linear operator, subspace, image/preimage, and bijection definitions supply each named construction.
Images and preimages of subspaces are proved closed under addition and scalar multiplication for a linear operator; operator, subspace, image, and preimage are exact hypotheses/results.
The indicator definition maps a subset to extended reals and explicitly identifies its domain and epigraph; extended-real, domain, and epigraph definitions are required.
The theorem states that interior and closure of a convex set in a normed space are convex; normed-space, convex-set, interior, and closure are all output or hypothesis concepts.
The first isomorphism theorem constructs X/ker(T) to im(T), with finite-dimensional codimension equality; image/kernel isomorphism, quotient, and linear map are the named inputs.
A nonzero linear functional has a kernel of codimension one; vector-space, linear-map, kernel/image, and quotient definitions supply the theorem statement.
The Legendre–Fenchel transform is the supremum pairing for an extended-real function; function, extended reals, supremum, and inner product are direct definition inputs.

triage_records.evidence: The theorem compares closure of interior with closure and interior of closure for a normed convex set with nonempty interior; normed-space, convex-set, interior, and closure are required. Added those omitted statement concepts.
The ball characterization states membership in the interior iff a metric ball is contained in the set; metric-space and interior are the two defining concepts. Added interior for the theorem output.
Interior is defined as the union of open subsets of a metric space; metric-space and open-subset are both defining inputs. Added open-subset.
The intersection of any family of linear subspaces is a subspace; vector-space is the ambient setting and linear-subspace is the family/result concept. Added vector-space.
The intersection of convex subsets is convex by applying the two-point definition in a vector space; vector-space and convex-set are direct inputs. Added vector-space.
The Legendre transform is defined for a differentiable strictly convex function on an open convex set and uses the gradient and Fenchel conjugate; added convex-set for the explicit domain hypothesis.
